extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers; essayists, moralists, and writers/composers interested in style and conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles embedded in early-18th-century essays on character, style, music, and public life; useful for writers of moral commentary, character sketches, and religious/occasional verse. Emphasises fidelity to nature, listening to local voices, and appropriate diction for elevated subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow Nature (obey one's natural talents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow Nature; build upon Nature — men should pursue the qualities and careers to which their natural genius or constitution inclines rather than affect characters for which they are unfit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay repeatedly counsels against affectation: do not force yourself into roles 'for which Nature never designed them.' Examples given: Cleanthes wastes talents by trying to be a 'fine Gentleman' instead of studying a profession; Valerio has no genius for poetry but persists in writing it; Cælia and Iras each neglect their natural excellences (beauty vs wit). The practical rule: 'To build upon Nature, is laying the Foundation upon a Rock' — graft upon and assist Nature, not oppose it. Anti-patterns: affectation, attempting vocations or styles unsuited to one's temperament (producing 'Coxcombs' and false characters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground public commentary in observed local voices
rubrics_metrics.description: When treating public or political affairs, inform oneself by hearing the reflections and speculations of people in different districts — the city is 'an Aggregate of various Nations' with distinct manners and interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer should 'ramble up and down a whole Day' to learn opinions from St. James's, Giles's, Jenny Man's, the Temple, Paul's Church-Yard, Cheapside, etc., placing oneself near the local 'statesman' of each coffee-house to learn the prevailing judgment. Use these distinct voices and particular interests to shape commentary—note how the same event (a foreign king's death) is taken up differently depending on the quarter (political theorists, French gentlemen, fishmongers worrying about mackerel, a haberdasher boasting prior prediction). Practical advice: collect and reflect varied perspectives; tailor observations to local concerns; examples of authentic colour (haberdasher, Temple disputants, Fish-street oracle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use solemn, scriptural diction to elevate religious music and poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: For divine songs, anthems, and devotional poetry, the Hebrew idioms and 'manners of speech' drawn from the Scriptures impart a particular grace, force, and energy to English expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: composers and poets should draw on the treasury of words and idioms from the Psalms and other sacred writings to give solemnity and ardour to devotional verse. The essay contrasts the comparative poverty of imagination in classical translations (Horace, Pindar) with the 'pathetick' diction of the Scriptures and suggests reading the Book of Psalms to learn these beauties. Practical implication: adopt more solemn, energetic phrasing (Hebraisms/solemn phraseology) when the aim is to stir devotion or to dignify worship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat music as a moral/religious art that purifies and exalts the passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Music — especially church music, hymns, and anthems — should serve both devotion and moral improvement by purifying and exalting the passions, making 'the Heart better' while giving pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author urges patrons and composers to encourage church music rather than only stage music: 'Pleasure and Duty go hand in hand.' Historical precedent: music among the chosen people was a religious art; drama itself originated in hymn-like chorus. Practical guidance for creators: choose subject matter and words for music that are praise-worthy and able to 'raise noble Hints in the Mind of the Hearer'; focus on compositions that strengthen devotion and produce lasting impressions rather than transient entertainments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make public recantation/repentance proportionate and visible in narrative devices
rubrics_metrics.description: When depicting repentance or seeking reconciliation in social/epistolary contexts, the author insists repentance should 'in some measure equal' the crime and, if the injury was public or notorious, the recantation should be visible and public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative/example: Amoret resolves to 'break through all Rules' and make her repentance so conspicuous that it may 'in some measure equal my Crime'; Philander responds that any recantation must be as well known as the original offense to be effective. Practical use in fiction/letters: use public letters, visible actions, or widely known gestures of apology when the plot requires believable reconciliation after a public wrong; the text treats public visibility of contrition as a necessary condition for restoring trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance solitude and public life in tone and subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid extreme praise of either solitude or public life; the best state is mixed — being useful in both private retirement and public affairs, like a gentle stream that 'glides through lonely Vales' but also 'visits populous Towns.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For writers and moralists: present characters and scenes that show the value of a moderate life; some persons are naturally suited to solitude and make better figures in obscurity, while others contribute publicly. Use this balance as a theme or organising principle in essays and character sketches. Anti-patterns: portraying solitude as uniformly isolating and public life as uniformly virtuous; instead, show the costs of extremes (rest leading to uselessness vs precipitation causing destruction).
